scenarios.title: Describe, don't instruct
scenarios.situation: Two scripts provision a VM: Script A runs 'create VM, then attach disk, then install nginx' as sequential API calls. Script B declares 'there shall be a VM with a disk running nginx' and the tool figures out the steps and order.
scenarios.prompt: Which is declarative IaC, and what practical advantage does it give on the second run?
choices: Script B — rerunning it converges to the desired state without duplicating resources (idempotent)
Script A — explicit steps are always safer than abstraction
Both are declarative — they both end with a VM running nginx
Script B — but it must be run exactly once or it duplicates everything
scenarios.why: Declarative IaC describes desired end state; the tool plans the actions and, crucially, compares current vs desired state on every run — creating only what's missing. Script A is imperative: rerunning it blindly would create a second VM. Idempotent convergence is what makes 'apply' safe to repeat.
scenarios.hint: What happens if you run each script twice?

scenarios.title: The hand-edited security group
scenarios.situation: Someone opens the cloud console and manually adds port 22 to a Terraform-managed security group during an incident. Weeks later, 'terraform plan' shows a change to remove that rule.
scenarios.prompt: What is this phenomenon, and how should the team handle it?
choices: Configuration drift — decide intentionally: codify the rule in Terraform if it's wanted, or let apply remove it; don't leave plan permanently dirty
State corruption — delete the state file and re-import everything
A Terraform bug — plan should ignore manual changes
Expected behavior — manual console changes are the recommended hotfix path
scenarios.why: Drift is any real-world change made outside Terraform. 'plan' detects it by refreshing state against reality. The fix is process: either the change was legitimate (then commit it to code so it's managed) or it wasn't (then apply reverts it). A permanently-dirty plan trains the team to ignore plans — dangerous.
scenarios.hint: Who is the source of truth — the console click or the code?

scenarios.title: Pets vs cattle
scenarios.situation: Server 'zeus-prod-01' has been hand-tuned over 3 years; nobody dares reboot it. The new platform team proposes replacing it with identical, disposable VMs built from code.
scenarios.prompt: What principle is the platform team applying, and what does it require?
choices: Immutable infrastructure / cattle-not-pets — servers are replaced, never modified; it requires everything about a server to be in code
Mutable infrastructure — keep tuning zeus in place
Serverless — delete all VMs immediately
High availability — just add a second hand-tuned server
scenarios.why: Pets are unique, hand-maintained, and irreplaceable; cattle are identical and disposable. Immutable infra means changes produce new images/instances rather than SSH-and-patch, which requires full codification (golden images or IaC) so any instance can be rebuilt identically. That's what makes zeus safely replaceable.
scenarios.hint: If zeus died tonight, could you rebuild it exactly? What would that take?

scenarios.title: Terraform or Ansible for the VM?
scenarios.situation: You need to (1) create 10 cloud VMs with networks and disks, and (2) install and configure the app on each. A teammate says 'just use Ansible for both' and another says 'just use Terraform for both'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic division of labor?
choices: Terraform provisions the infrastructure (VMs, networks, disks); Ansible configures the software on them — provisioning vs configuration management
Ansible for both — Terraform can't manage cloud resources
Terraform for both — provisioners make it a full config management tool
It doesn't matter — they are interchangeable
scenarios.why: Terraform excels at provisioning: declarative lifecycle of infrastructure resources with state. Ansible excels at configuration: converging machine state (packages, files, services) via SSH/WinRM. Terraform provisioners exist but are a last resort — the tools are complementary, and most stacks use both in sequence.
scenarios.hint: Which tool keeps a state file of cloud resources, and which converges files and services on a host?

scenarios.title: Justifying IaC to the skeptics
scenarios.situation: A manager asks why the team should rewrite working click-ops runbooks as Terraform code: 'The console works fine and we've done it for years.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest business case?
choices: Code gives versioned, peer-reviewed, repeatable, auditable infrastructure — environments can be reproduced and changes reviewed like software
Terraform is faster to click through than the console
IaC eliminates the need for any operations staff
Cloud providers require Terraform for all resources
scenarios.why: The case is software-engineering discipline applied to infra: git history (who changed what, when), pull-request review, repeatable environments (dev/staging/prod parity), disaster recovery (rebuild from code), and audit trails. It's about risk and repeatability, not click speed — and it doesn't eliminate ops, it elevates them.
scenarios.hint: What do you get when infrastructure changes go through pull requests?

scenarios.title: Patching the fleet in place
scenarios.situation: Security mandates a critical OS patch on 200 VMs by Friday. The team debates: SSH into each and patch in place, vs build a new patched image and roll out fresh VMs.
scenarios.prompt: Compare the approaches on risk and rollback.
choices: In-place patching is faster to start but each host can diverge and rollback is painful; immutable rollout (new image, blue-green) is atomic with instant rollback to the old fleet
In-place patching is always safer because the hosts are already proven
Immutable rollout means you can never patch — you must rebuild for CVEs only
Both are identical in risk; pick whichever is less typing
scenarios.why: Mutable patching risks snowflake drift (failed patches, half-applied updates) and rollback means un-patching. Immutable/blue-green treats the patched image as the unit: roll forward by shifting traffic, roll back by shifting it back — the old fleet stays intact until the new one is verified. The cost is image-build pipeline investment.
scenarios.hint: If the patch breaks the app, which approach gets you back fastest?

scenarios.title: First plan shows 12 resources
scenarios.situation: You wrote your first Terraform configuration for a small web stack: a VPC, two subnets, a security group, and an EC2 instance. You run 'terraform plan' and it shows 12 resources to add. You expected 5.
scenarios.prompt: What best explains the plan output?
evidence:
terraform plan
Plan: 12 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
  + aws_vpc.main
  + aws_subnet.public_a
  + aws_subnet.public_b
  + aws_security_group.web
  + aws_instance.web
  + aws_internet_gateway.igw
  ...
choices: Your resources have implicit dependencies that pull in supporting resources (internet gateway, route tables, associations) — plan shows the full graph, which is correct.
Terraform duplicated your resources; delete the .terraform directory and re-run init to fix the count.
The state file is corrupt and Terraform is planning phantom resources — run 'terraform refresh' to clear it.
Plan counts each attribute as a resource; the real number is 5 and the display is misleading.
scenarios.why: Terraform builds a dependency graph from resource references — an internet gateway, route tables, and route-table associations are real resources your config declares (directly or via references), not duplicates. 'terraform plan' always shows the complete set of actions. Deleting .terraform only removes provider plugins; refresh updates state from reality.
scenarios.hint: Look at the resource type names in the plan — are they copies of your five, or different kinds of infrastructure?

scenarios.title: Name that block
scenarios.situation: A new file mixes up block types: a 'resource' fetching data, a 'data' block creating a VM, and variables declared inside a resource.
scenarios.prompt: What is each top-level block type actually for?
choices: resource: manages (creates/updates/deletes) infrastructure; data: reads existing info; variable: declares inputs at top level; output/locals/terraform/provider/module complete the set
resource and data are interchangeable — the names are cosmetic
Variables must be declared inside the resource that uses them
Only resource blocks are real — the rest are comments
scenarios.why: HCL block types have fixed roles: terraform (version/backend), provider, resource (managed objects, the only ones in state as managed), data (read-only lookups evaluated at plan), variable (inputs), output (exposed values), locals (computed helpers), module (composition). Swapping resource/data inverts manage-vs-read semantics.
scenarios.hint: Which block creates things, and which only reads?

scenarios.title: Three subnets, one block
scenarios.situation: You need three subnets from a map of {a: '10.0.1.0/24', b: '10.0.2.0/24', c: '10.0.3.0/24'}. Using count=3 with element() works, but removing subnet 'b' later renumbers everything and forces recreation.
scenarios.prompt: Why is for_each the better choice here?
choices: for_each keys instances by map key (a/b/c) — removing 'b' only destroys that instance; count keys by index, so removals shift every later instance
for_each is faster — count is deprecated
count can't be used with maps at all
They're identical — the recreation was a bug
scenarios.why: count addresses instances by position (aws_subnet.x[0..2]); removing a middle element shifts indices, so Terraform sees changed identities and recreates. for_each addresses by key (aws_subnet.x["b"]), making each instance's identity stable. Rule: for_each for maps/sets of named things, count for N identical copies.
scenarios.hint: What identifies each instance — its position, or its name?

scenarios.title: Validating inputs early
scenarios.situation: A module takes 'instance_type' as a string. Someone passes 't2.microo' (typo) and the failure surfaces 8 minutes into apply as a cloud API error.
scenarios.prompt: How do you catch this at plan time?
choices: Add a validation block on the variable with a condition (e.g., regex or contains(list)) — failures surface during plan before anything is created
Validation isn't possible — Terraform variables accept anything
Use a local instead of a variable — locals are validated
Catch it in CI with grep on the tfvars file
scenarios.why: variable blocks support type constraints (string, number, list(string), object({...})) and validation { condition, error_message } blocks evaluated at plan. Type constraints catch shape errors; validation catches value errors. Failing fast at plan is the whole point — never discover a typo via a half-applied infrastructure change.
scenarios.hint: Where can you declare 'this input must look like X' so plan fails fast?

scenarios.title: Don't hardcode the AMI
scenarios.situation: Your config hardcodes ami-0abc123 (Ubuntu 22.04 in us-east-1). In eu-west-1 the ID doesn't exist, and when Canonical publishes a patched AMI you want it automatically.
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic lookup?
choices: data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" with most_recent=true and filters for name/virtualization-type — resolved at plan, portable across regions
Keep hardcoding — AMI IDs are global
Use a variable with the AMI per region — data sources can't query AMIs
data blocks run at apply, so they can't help planning
scenarios.why: Data sources read existing infrastructure/objects at plan time. data.aws_ami with filters (e.g., name = "ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd/ubuntu-jammy-22.04-*") plus most_recent picks the latest matching AMI in whatever region the provider targets — no hardcoded IDs, automatic patch pickup. Then reference data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id.
scenarios.hint: Which block type reads rather than creates?

scenarios.title: The remote-exec habit
scenarios.situation: A config uses remote-exec provisioners to apt-get install packages and write config files on every VM. Applies are flaky: SSH timeouts fail the whole apply, and reruns reinstall everything.
scenarios.prompt: What is HashiCorp's stance, and what's the better pattern?
choices: Provisioners are a last resort — bake config into images (Packer) or hand off to a config tool; provisioners run outside Terraform's state model and aren't idempotent
Provisioners are the recommended way to configure VMs
Add more provisioners — redundancy fixes flakiness
Provisioners only fail because of the network — retry logic fixes it
scenarios.why: HashiCorp docs call provisioners a last resort: they execute imperatively outside the declarative model, can't be planned, and failures leave tainted resources. Better: build immutable images with Packer (install once, deploy many), use cloud-init/user_data for boot-time config, or pair Terraform (provision) with Ansible (configure). null_resource + local-exec is for glue, not config.
scenarios.hint: What does Terraform know about the state of things a provisioner changed?

scenarios.title: Computed names everywhere
scenarios.situation: Resources need names like 'prod-api-ue1-004' built from environment, service, region code, and index. The expression is copy-pasted in 12 places and one copy has a typo.
scenarios.prompt: How do you define it once?
choices: locals { name_prefix = "${var.env}-${var.service}-${var.region_code}" } then reference local.name_prefix everywhere; expose key results via output blocks
Variables can compute from other variables — just use var.name_prefix
Copy-paste is fine — DRY doesn't apply to HCL
Use a data source to compute strings
scenarios.why: locals define named computed expressions evaluated within the module — the DRY mechanism for derived values. Variables can't reference other variables (inputs only). outputs expose values to parent modules or the CLI (terraform output). Together: variables in, locals compute, resources consume, outputs publish.
scenarios.hint: Which block exists specifically for expressions computed from other values?

scenarios.title: Rename Without Rebuild
scenarios.situation: You rename `aws_instance.web` to `aws_instance.web_a` for clarity. The next plan wants to destroy the production instance and create a new one.
scenarios.prompt: How do you rename safely?
evidence: Plan: 1 to add, 1 to destroy (aws_instance.web -> aws_instance.web_a)
the instance holds production data on its root volume
choices: Add a `moved` block (`moved { from = aws_instance.web, to = aws_instance.web_a }`): Terraform updates the state address with zero infrastructure changes, then apply
Use `terraform state mv` — but only as a manual one-off; `moved` blocks are the declarative, reviewable equivalent
Let it destroy and recreate; the data is on EBS so it's safe
Rename it back; resource addresses can never change
scenarios.why: `moved` blocks make refactoring declarative and code-reviewable: state is rewritten, infrastructure untouched. `terraform state mv` works but is imperative and invisible in PRs. Destroy/recreate for a rename is never acceptable on stateful resources.
scenarios.hint: What tells Terraform 'same object, new address'?

scenarios.title: Data Source or Resource?
scenarios.situation: A module needs the ID of the company's existing shared VPC and the latest Amazon Linux AMI. A teammate wrote `resource "aws_vpc" "shared"` and `resource "aws_ami" "latest"` and plans to manage them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct construct?
evidence: vpc-0abc123 owned by the network team; must not be modified
would try to CREATE a new VPC
choices: Use `data` sources (`data "aws_vpc" "shared"` with filters, `data "aws_ami"` with most_recent): data sources read existing infrastructure without managing it — resources would attempt to create/own it
Keep resources but add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`; that makes them read-only
Hardcode the IDs as variables; data sources are slower
Import the shared VPC into this configuration's state
scenarios.why: Resources = Terraform owns the lifecycle. Data sources = Terraform reads what someone else owns. Managing shared infrastructure from an app config risks accidental modification; importing it duplicates ownership across states.
scenarios.hint: Who owns the lifecycle of that VPC?

scenarios.title: Why does Terraform need a state file?
scenarios.situation: A newcomer asks why 'terraform apply' needs terraform.tfstate — 'can't it just read the config and the cloud?'
scenarios.prompt: What three jobs does state perform?
choices: Maps config resources to real-world IDs, caches metadata for performance, and enables drift detection (comparing desired vs actual)
State is just a log file — it can be deleted freely
State stores your cloud credentials
State is only needed for destroy — apply works without it
scenarios.why: State is the binding between your configuration and reality: resource X in code ↔ i-0abc123 in AWS. Without it, Terraform can't plan updates (it wouldn't know what exists), detects drift by refreshing state against APIs, and caches attributes to avoid re-reading everything. Deleting state orphans real resources (they still exist and bill you, but Terraform forgets them).
scenarios.hint: How would Terraform know that 'aws_instance.web' already exists as i-0abc123?

scenarios.title: Two engineers, one state file
scenarios.situation: Two engineers run apply against local terraform.tfstate on a shared drive. One's apply overwrites the other's; resources get orphaned.
scenarios.prompt: What is the proper remote-state setup?
choices: A backend block (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB locking, or Terraform Cloud remote) — shared storage plus state locking so only one apply runs at a time
Email the state file back and forth — simple and effective
Each engineer keeps their own state — duplication is safe
Delete state after each apply — fresh starts avoid conflicts
scenarios.why: Backends store state remotely (S3, GCS, AzureRM, Terraform Cloud) with locking (DynamoDB table, native mechanisms) that serializes applies — the second apply waits or fails cleanly instead of corrupting. Backend config can't use variables (it's needed before variables are evaluated); use -backend-config or partial configuration. Never share local state files.
scenarios.hint: What prevents two applies from writing state simultaneously?

scenarios.title: Adopting the hand-built VM
scenarios.situation: A production VM was built by hand in the console. You want it under Terraform management without recreating it (downtime is unacceptable).
scenarios.prompt: What is the adoption workflow?
choices: Write the resource block, then 'terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abc123' — then run plan and reconcile config until plan is clean
terraform apply will discover the VM automatically
Delete the VM and let Terraform recreate it — import is deprecated
Copy the console settings into a tfvars file — that's the import
scenarios.why: import binds an existing real-world object to a resource address in state — it doesn't generate config. The workflow: write the resource block (matching reality as closely as possible), import, then iterate 'plan' until no changes (config now describes reality). For bulk adoption, config-driven import blocks (import { to, id }) in Terraform 1.5+ make it reviewable in code.
scenarios.hint: Does import create the config, or only link reality to an address?

scenarios.title: Renaming without recreating
scenarios.situation: You rename a resource from aws_instance.old to aws_instance.web in config. Plan wants to destroy and recreate the VM — unacceptable downtime.
scenarios.prompt: How do you tell Terraform it's the same object?
choices: 'terraform state mv aws_instance.old aws_instance.web' — renames the state address without touching the real resource; or use a moved {} block in config
Rename it and accept the recreation — renames always recreate
Edit terraform.tfstate JSON by hand — fastest
taint the resource — taint preserves the VM
scenarios.why: State addresses are how Terraform tracks identity — renaming the block changes the address, so plan sees delete+create. 'state mv' (or the declarative moved { from, to } block, which is code-reviewable and applies on next plan) updates the address in place. Never hand-edit state JSON; use the commands. (taint forces recreation — the opposite.)
scenarios.hint: What does Terraform think happened when the address changes?

scenarios.title: Dev and prod from one config
scenarios.situation: You need dev and prod environments from the same configuration with separate state. Someone suggests workspaces; someone else suggests separate directories.
scenarios.prompt: When is each appropriate?
choices: Workspaces (terraform workspace new prod) suit near-identical envs differing by variables; separate configs/directories suit envs with structural differences
Workspaces are deprecated — always use directories
Directories are deprecated — always use workspaces
Both are identical — pick randomly
scenarios.why: Workspaces are named state instances for one backend/config — 'terraform.workspace' interpolates names per env. They work when environments are structurally identical and differ only in inputs. When envs diverge (different resources, backends, access controls), separate directories/configurations (or separate backend keys) give cleaner isolation and blast-radius control.
scenarios.hint: Do your environments differ in values, or in structure?

scenarios.title: Secrets in the state file
scenarios.situation: You output a database password. It's now in terraform.tfstate in plaintext — and in the S3 backend, and in every plan log.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle sensitive values in state?
choices: Mark variables/outputs sensitive=true (redacts console/UI), encrypt the backend at rest, restrict state access tightly — and prefer secret stores over Terraform-managed secrets
sensitive=true encrypts the state file — problem solved
State never contains secrets — outputs are safe
Delete the state file — the secret goes with it
scenarios.why: sensitive = true only redacts display (CLI output, UI) — the value still sits in state plaintext. Real protection: backend encryption at rest, strict IAM on the state bucket, and avoiding secrets-in-Terraform where possible (use Vault/AWS Secrets Manager with Terraform referencing them, or Ephemeral values where supported). Anyone with state read access has your secrets.
scenarios.hint: Does 'sensitive' encrypt anything, or just hide display?

scenarios.title: State file on a laptop
scenarios.situation: Two engineers run 'terraform apply' from their laptops against the same infrastructure. Last week both applied within minutes of each other and the state file diverged — resources were created twice and billing spiked.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
evidence:
ls terraform.tfstate*
terraform.tfstate  terraform.tfstate.backup
# no backend block in any .tf file
choices: Configure a remote backend (e.g. S3 with DynamoDB locking, Terraform Cloud, or equivalent) so state is shared and applies are serialized with locking.
Have the engineers coordinate over chat before each apply so they never run at the same time.
Copy the state file to a shared drive after every apply so both laptops stay in sync.
Run 'terraform apply -auto-approve' faster so the window for collision shrinks.
scenarios.why: Local state cannot be shared or locked — concurrent applies race and corrupt it. A remote backend centralizes the state file and provides a lock (DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, etc.) so only one apply mutates at a time. Chat coordination and file copies are racy and unauditable.
scenarios.hint: The state file is the single source of truth. What happens when two writers share one file with no lock?

scenarios.title: Someone changed it in the console
scenarios.situation: A teammate manually changed a security group rule in the cloud console during an incident. Now 'terraform plan' wants to revert that change, but the incident fix must stay until the postmortem next week.
scenarios.prompt: How should you handle the drift?
evidence:
terraform plan
  ~ aws_security_group_rule.incident
      - cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] -> null   # forces replacement? no, in-place update
Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
choices: Codify the incident change in the Terraform configuration (update the rule to match reality), so config and state agree and the change is tracked in version control.
Run 'terraform apply -refresh-only' to make the plan go away without changing anything.
Delete the resource from state with 'terraform state rm' so Terraform stops managing it.
Edit terraform.tfstate by hand to match the console change.
scenarios.why: Drift means reality and config disagree; the durable fix is to make the config describe reality so the change is reviewed, versioned, and reproducible. -refresh-only updates state to match reality but leaves config wrong, so the next real plan re-proposes the revert. state rm abandons management; hand-editing state is dangerous and unaudited.
scenarios.hint: The console change is legitimate for now. Where should a legitimate infrastructure change live so it survives?

scenarios.title: The tainted database
scenarios.situation: A database instance is in a bad state after a failed upgrade — Terraform didn't create the problem, but the instance needs replacement. 'terraform apply' reports no changes because config matches state.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to force replacement of just that resource?
evidence:
terraform plan
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
# but db-primary is corrupted and must be rebuilt
choices: Run 'terraform apply -replace=aws_db_instance.primary' to taint-equivalent replace only that resource on the next apply.
Delete the resource from the state file so Terraform recreates it.
Change a random attribute in the config to trick Terraform into replacing it, then change it back.
Run 'terraform destroy' followed by 'terraform apply' to rebuild everything cleanly.
scenarios.why: '-replace' (the modern replacement for 'terraform taint') marks a single resource for destroy-and-recreate on the next apply without touching anything else. Destroying everything rebuilds healthy resources unnecessarily; config tricks leave confusing history; manual state edits risk corruption.
scenarios.hint: You need exactly one resource destroyed and recreated. Which flag targets a single resource address for replacement?

scenarios.title: Workspace or separate state?
scenarios.situation: You need dev, staging, and prod environments. A colleague suggests Terraform workspaces ('terraform workspace new prod') with one backend. Your prod environment requires separate credentials, stricter approvals, and must never share state with dev.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach is appropriate?
evidence:
terraform workspace list
* default
# backend: single S3 bucket, one key prefix
choices: Use separate backend configurations (separate state files/paths, e.g. per-environment directories or distinct backend keys) rather than workspaces, since prod needs isolation of credentials, state, and blast radius.
Use workspaces — they are designed for environment separation and keep everything in one configuration.
Use one workspace and gate prod with '-target' so only prod resources apply.
Put all environments in one state file and rely on naming conventions to tell them apart.
scenarios.why: Workspaces share one backend configuration and are easy to confuse ('which workspace am I in?' mistakes have destroyed prod). When environments need different credentials, approvals, and hard isolation, separate state files per environment (separate directories or backend keys) give real blast-radius separation. -target is a surgical tool, not an environment strategy.
scenarios.hint: Workspaces are a convenience for lightweight variants. What breaks if someone forgets which workspace is selected before a destroy?

scenarios.title: Two Applies, One State
scenarios.situation: Two engineers run `terraform apply` at the same time against a local `terraform.tfstate`. The second apply corrupts the state file and both runs partially create resources.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct state setup?
evidence: none configured — terraform.tfstate in the repo directory
Error: Failed to save state: state lock timeout / state file truncated
choices: Configure a remote backend (e.g. S3 with versioning + DynamoDB state locking, or Terraform Cloud): the backend serializes access with a lock so concurrent applies queue instead of corrupting state
Add `terraform.tfstate` to `.gitignore`; local state is fine if it's ignored
Tell engineers to coordinate applies over chat; locking is overkill
Run applies with `-parallelism=1`; that serializes concurrent runs
scenarios.why: Local state has no locking — concurrent writes corrupt it. Remote backends provide atomic state operations plus a lock (DynamoDB, or native in TFC/HCP). -parallelism only limits resource concurrency within one run, not across runs.
scenarios.hint: What serializes two separate terraform processes?

scenarios.title: Drift on Autopilot
scenarios.situation: Nightly `terraform plan` shows the same 3-line diff: someone keeps widening a security group in the console for debugging and forgetting to revert. The team wants the config to win automatically.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct drift strategy?
evidence: break-glass console access must remain possible
choices: Keep Terraform as the source of truth and re-apply on a schedule (or enable HCP Terraform drift detection with notifications): the next apply reverts the console change; document break-glass as temporary and time-boxed
Add `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [ingress] }` so the plan stays clean
Delete the security group from the config; manage it only in the console
Run `terraform refresh` nightly; that reverts console changes
scenarios.why: ignore_changes surrenders the security group to ClickOps permanently — the config lies about reality. Scheduled applies (or HCP drift detection + auto-apply) make the declared state win while keeping break-glass possible. refresh only updates state to match reality; it changes nothing in the cloud.
scenarios.hint: Do you want the config to describe reality, or reality to match the config?

scenarios.title: Calling the VPC module
scenarios.situation: The registry has terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws. You need a VPC with 3 AZs, version pinned, in your root config.
scenarios.prompt: What does the module block look like?
choices: module "vpc" { source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"; version = "~> 5.0"; name = "prod"; cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"; azs = [...]; ... }
resource "module" "vpc" { registry = "vpc" } — modules are resources
import "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws" — modules are imported like code
Modules can't be versioned — source pins are enough
scenarios.why: module blocks: source (registry address namespace/name/provider, git URL, or local path) + version constraint (registry modules only) + input variables. Version pinning (~> 5.0 = >=5.0, <6.0) keeps applies deterministic; dependabot/renovate can bump. Reference outputs as module.vpc.vpc_id.
scenarios.hint: Which two arguments identify exactly which module code to use?

scenarios.title: Designing a module's interface
scenarios.situation: You're writing a reusable 'app-service' module. Users keep asking 'what inputs does it take and what does it give back'.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a module's interface clear?
choices: variables.tf with typed variables, descriptions, defaults/validations + outputs.tf with described outputs + README documenting the contract
Modules don't need interfaces — users read the resources
Put all inputs as locals — simpler
One giant main.tf with comments — structure is overhead
scenarios.why: A module is an API: variables.tf declares the contract (type, description, default, validation), outputs.tf publishes results (with descriptions, sensitive flags). This is what registry docs render. Keep the interface small and stable; internals (main.tf) can churn. Version the module so interface changes are explicit.
scenarios.hint: What two files define a module's inputs and outputs?

scenarios.title: One module, three environments
scenarios.situation: You want the app-service module instantiated for dev, staging, prod with different inputs. Copy-pasting the module block thrice works but adding a fourth env means more copy-paste.
scenarios.prompt: How do you instantiate a module per map entry?
choices: for_each = var.envs on the module block, keyed by env name — each instance addressable as module.app["prod"]
count = 3 — modules don't support for_each
Modules can't be looped — use workspaces instead
Write a wrapper module per environment — that's the pattern
scenarios.why: Module blocks support for_each (and count): for_each over a map gives stable keyed instances (module.app["prod"]), so adding/removing envs only affects that instance. Note: modules with for_each can't be targeted as granularly in older versions, and their outputs become maps — design consumers accordingly.
scenarios.hint: Which meta-argument do resources use for keyed multiples — and do modules support it too?

scenarios.title: Private module, no registry
scenarios.situation: Your org's modules live in a private GitHub repo, no Terraform Cloud private registry. Teams need to consume them with version pinning.
scenarios.prompt: What source syntax works?
choices: source = "git::https://github.com/org/tf-modules.git//vpc?ref=v2.1.0" — git source with subdir and ref pin
Modules must come from the public registry — private isn't possible
Copy the module directory into every repo — vendoring is required
Use the registry source with a private token in source
scenarios.why: Generic git sources: git::URL//subdir?ref=<tag/branch/commit> — ref pins the version (use tags, not branches, for stability). Also supported: local paths (./modules/vpc, no versioning), S3/GCS archives, Terraform Cloud private registry. 'terraform init' fetches and caches them in .terraform/.
scenarios.hint: How do you point at a subdirectory of a git repo at a specific tag?

scenarios.title: Module calling module
scenarios.situation: Your app module internally calls the vpc module. A user of the app module asks which version of the vpc module they'll get.
scenarios.prompt: How does versioning work for nested modules, and what's the guidance?
choices: Nested modules resolve their own source/version independently — keep nesting shallow and pin versions at every level to avoid surprise upgrades
The root module's version pins cascade to nested modules
Nested modules are forbidden — flatten everything
Versions don't matter for nested modules — they're internal
scenarios.why: Each module block's source+version stands alone; there's no inheritance of version constraints down the tree. Deep nesting hides version decisions from the root author. Guidance: prefer flat composition (root calls vpc + app), keep shared logic in small leaf modules, and pin versions everywhere so 'terraform init -upgrade' is a deliberate act.
scenarios.hint: Does a version constraint in the root apply to modules called by your modules?

scenarios.title: Reading ~> 2.4.0
scenarios.situation: A module pins version = "~> 2.4.0". A teammate reads it as 'exactly 2.4.0' and another as 'any 2.x'.
scenarios.prompt: What does the pessimistic constraint actually allow?
choices: >= 2.4.0, < 2.5.0 — allows patch-level updates within 2.4, blocks 2.5.0+
Exactly 2.4.0 — no updates allowed
It's invalid syntax — constraints use only >= and <=
scenarios.why: The pessimistic operator ~> allows the rightmost specified component to increment: ~> 2.4.0 → >=2.4.0, <2.5.0; ~> 2.4 → >=2.4, <3.0. It's the standard 'take compatible fixes, not features' pin. Combine constraints with commas (">= 2.0, < 2.5"). The lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) then pins the exact selected versions per working directory.
scenarios.hint: Which version component is allowed to change under ~> 2.4.0?

scenarios.title: Module or copy-paste?
scenarios.situation: Your team deploys the same three-tier stack in dev, staging, and prod. Today each environment is a full copy of 600 lines of HCL, and a tagging-standard change means editing three files identically.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best refactor?
evidence:
ls environments/
dev/main.tf  staging/main.tf  prod/main.tf   # 600 lines each, near-identical
diff environments/dev/main.tf environments/staging/main.tf | wc -l
23
choices: Extract the stack into a reusable module with input variables (name, instance size, tags), and have each environment call the module with its own values.
Use symlinks so all three environments share one main.tf file.
Keep the copies but write a script that copies dev/main.tf over the others after each change.
Merge all environments into one configuration with count-based duplication.
scenarios.why: Modules are Terraform's reuse mechanism: one implementation, parameterized per environment via variables, so a tagging change is made once. Symlinks and copy scripts destroy per-environment independence; merging environments into one config couples their lifecycles and blast radius.
scenarios.hint: The three files differ in 23 lines — those differences are parameters. What construct turns repeated config into a parameterized unit?

scenarios.title: The daily driver loop
scenarios.situation: You clone an existing Terraform repo on a new laptop. Nothing is initialized. You need to get to a safe apply.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct command sequence, and what does each do?
choices: terraform init (install providers/modules, configure backend) → terraform plan (preview changes) → terraform apply (execute after review)
terraform apply directly — init and plan are optional
terraform plan first — it also initializes
terraform validate replaces init — just validate and apply
scenarios.why: init prepares the working directory (provider binaries, module sources, backend init — rerun after config changes); plan shows the create/update/delete diff for review (the safety gate); apply executes (prompts for confirmation unless -auto-approve). validate/fmt are hygiene steps inside the loop: fmt -check in CI, validate for syntax.
scenarios.hint: Which step downloads providers, which previews, which executes?

scenarios.title: Plan today, apply tomorrow
scenarios.situation: Change review board approves the plan on Monday; the apply window is Wednesday. You must guarantee Wednesday's apply does exactly what was approved.
scenarios.prompt: How do you lock the plan?
choices: terraform plan -out=tfplan (binary plan file), then terraform apply tfplan — applies exactly the saved plan, failing if state drifted
Save the plan text output and re-run plan Wednesday — text is binding
Plans are automatically saved — just apply Wednesday
Email the plan output — that's the lock
scenarios.why: 'plan -out' serializes the full planned changeset; 'apply <file>' executes that exact plan (it errors if the state changed underneath, preventing unreviewed drift from sneaking in). This is the change-management pattern: review the human-readable plan, approve the artifact, apply the artifact. Never 'apply' a fresh plan in a gated window.
scenarios.hint: What makes an approved plan binding instead of advisory?

scenarios.title: One bad VM in a big apply
scenarios.situation: A 50-resource apply has one corrupted VM. You want to recreate just that VM — not re-run everything, and not hand-delete it.
scenarios.prompt: What are the surgical options, and the caution?
choices: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.bad — recreates that resource on next apply; -target is the broader escape hatch for exceptional use only
terraform taint is the modern way — -replace is deprecated
Delete it in the console — Terraform will notice
-target everything except the VM — safest
scenarios.why: -replace=<addr> marks one resource for destroy+create (taint's successor — 'terraform taint' is deprecated in favor of -replace). -target limits the apply to specific resources — powerful but dangerous: it skips everything else, leaving the rest unmanaged for that run and risking partial-state surprises. Use -target only for exceptional recovery, never as routine workflow.
scenarios.hint: Which flag recreates one resource, and which narrows the whole apply?

scenarios.title: The lock file in git?
scenarios.situation: A PR adds .terraform.lock.hcl. A teammate says 'lock files are local junk — gitignore it.'
scenarios.prompt: Who is right?
choices: Commit it — the lock file pins exact provider versions/hashes so every engineer and CI installs identical providers (supply-chain protection too)
Gitignore it — providers update automatically anyway
Commit it only for modules, not root configs
Lock files are Windows-only — irrelevant on Linux
scenarios.why: .terraform.lock.hcl records the selected provider versions with hashes (like package-lock.json). Committing it makes installs deterministic and tamper-evident across the team/CI. 'terraform init -upgrade' deliberately bumps; otherwise init respects the lock. It's the reproducibility + supply-chain story for providers.
scenarios.hint: What guarantees CI installs the same provider build you tested with?

scenarios.title: Terraform in CI/CD
scenarios.situation: You need a pipeline: PRs show the plan, merges to main apply automatically. Credentials must not live in the repo.
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard pipeline shape?
choices: PR: init → validate → plan (post output as PR comment); merge: plan -out → apply with approval gate; credentials via OIDC/secret manager, state in remote backend
Apply on every PR — fast feedback
Store cloud credentials in tfvars — convenient
Skip plan in CI — developers run it locally
scenarios.why: The GitOps-for-Terraform pattern: speculative plans on PRs (Atlantis, Terraform Cloud VCS runs, or CI jobs) give reviewers the diff; merge triggers the real apply, often with a manual approval step for prod. Cloud auth via OIDC federation (no static keys); plan artifacts passed between jobs. Drift-detection schedules (nightly plan) catch console changes.
scenarios.hint: When should a human see the plan — before or after merge?

scenarios.title: Terraform version drift
scenarios.situation: CI uses Terraform 1.9, your laptop has 1.5. A plan made on one fails on the other with state-format complaints.
scenarios.prompt: How do you pin the toolchain version in code?
choices: terraform { required_version = ">= 1.5, < 1.10" } plus required_providers — fails fast with a clear error on mismatch
Version pinning isn't possible — everyone must memorize the version
required_version goes in each resource block
Only the CI version matters — local doesn't
scenarios.why: The terraform block's required_version constrains the CLI (and required_providers pins provider sources/versions). Mismatches fail immediately with a clear message instead of cryptic state errors. Pair with a version manager (tfenv) or containerized runs so the whole team + CI converge on one version.
scenarios.hint: Which block declares 'this config needs Terraform >= X'?

scenarios.title: Adopting the ClickOps VPC
scenarios.situation: The networking team built the production VPC by hand in the console. You must bring it under Terraform management without recreating it (recreation would drop production traffic).
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct adoption sequence?
choices: Write resource blocks matching the real infrastructure, run `terraform import aws_vpc.main vpc-0abc123` (and the subnets/IGW), then `terraform plan` and reconcile config until the plan is empty — only then manage it normally
Write the config and run `terraform apply`; Terraform detects existing resources automatically
Delete the hand-built VPC and let Terraform recreate it cleanly
Use `terraform refresh` to generate the .tf files automatically
scenarios.why: Import binds real infrastructure to resource addresses without touching it; the following plan shows every config-vs-reality mismatch to fix before the first managed apply. Apply-without-import would try to create duplicates (or fail on name clashes); refresh only updates state, never writes config.
scenarios.hint: Which command binds an existing real object to a resource address?

scenarios.title: The Friday Afternoon Apply
scenarios.situation: A `terraform apply` to production on a Friday needs a second pair of eyes and a policy check (no public S3 buckets), but today anyone with AWS keys can apply directly from a laptop.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct collaboration control?
evidence: local applies from laptops; no review gate
a public bucket shipped last month
choices: Move runs to HCP Terraform / Terraform Cloud with VCS-driven speculative plans on every PR, required approvals before apply, and a Sentinel/OPA policy set denying public buckets — the plan becomes the review artifact
Require engineers to paste `terraform plan` output into Slack for approval
Restrict AWS IAM so nobody can apply; only read
Run `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` in CI and eyeball it
scenarios.why: HCP Terraform/TFC gives the three controls that matter: speculative plans on PRs (reviewable diff), run approvals (second pair of eyes), and policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA) enforced before apply. Chat-based approval is unauditable; plan output in CI without enforcement is advisory.
scenarios.hint: Where should the policy be enforced: in a human's eyes or in the run pipeline?

scenarios.title: Nightly drift detection
scenarios.situation: Someone keeps tweaking the load balancer in the console. You want automated detection with a report every morning — without auto-applying.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build drift detection with Terraform?
choices: Scheduled CI job running terraform plan -detailed-exitcode (exit 2 = changes) and posting the output — detection without apply
terraform apply nightly — auto-fixes drift
Drift can't be detected — only prevented
Delete the console access — detection is unnecessary
scenarios.why: 'plan -detailed-exitcode' returns 0 (no changes), 1 (error), or 2 (changes present) — perfect for scheduled jobs that alert on 2 and attach the plan. This detects drift without the risk of auto-apply. Pair with a policy: legitimate changes get codified (PR), the rest get reverted by a human-approved apply.
scenarios.hint: Which plan flag turns 'are there changes' into an exit code?

scenarios.title: Plans as PR comments
scenarios.situation: Developers propose infra changes via PRs but can't run Terraform locally (no credentials). Reviewers need to see the plan before approving.
scenarios.prompt: What workflow gives PR-based Terraform collaboration?
choices: Atlantis (or Terraform Cloud VCS runs): listens for PRs, runs plan automatically, posts the output as a PR comment, applies on merge after approval
Give every developer prod credentials — fastest
Review HCL by eye — plans aren't needed
Email tf files around — PRs are overkill
scenarios.why: Atlantis (open source) / Terraform Cloud / Spacelift implement the GitOps loop for Terraform: PR → automated plan comment → review → merge (+ optional apply). Credentials stay server-side; developers get full plan visibility without local access. It also serializes applies with locking — no concurrent-apply corruption.
scenarios.hint: What runs the plan when the author can't?

scenarios.title: Terraform + Argo CD: who owns what?
scenarios.situation: You use Terraform for AWS infrastructure AND Argo CD for Kubernetes apps. The team is confused about which tool manages the EKS cluster itself vs the apps on it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the clean separation?
choices: Terraform owns the platform (VPC, EKS cluster, node groups, cluster addons); Argo CD owns what runs ON it (app manifests) — Terraform can bootstrap Argo CD itself
One tool must do everything — pick one
Argo CD should create the EKS cluster — it manages infrastructure
Terraform should deploy app manifests — Argo CD is redundant
scenarios.why: Separation of concerns: Terraform (with its state model) provisions cloud/platform resources including the cluster; GitOps (Argo CD/Flux) continuously reconciles in-cluster desired state from git. Terraform's kubernetes provider CAN manage in-cluster objects, but fighting Argo CD's reconciler causes thrash — let each own its layer. Terraform bootstraps the GitOps agent as the handoff.
scenarios.hint: Which tool reconciles continuously, and which provisions with state?

scenarios.title: Secrets in the Terraform repo
scenarios.situation: Terraform needs a database password to create the DB, and the app needs it at runtime. The password is currently in tfvars, committed to git.
scenarios.prompt: What is the secrets-safe pattern?
choices: Generate with random_password (never in git), store in a secret manager (Vault/AWS Secrets Manager) via Terraform, and have apps read from the manager — Terraform never persists human-chosen secrets
Commit tfvars — the repo is private
Use default passwords — rotation is overrated
Put the password in the Terraform state only — state is safe
scenarios.why: The pattern: random_password generates (stored in state — protect state!), the secret manager holds it (rotation-capable), apps consume via the manager (never via Terraform outputs to humans). Human-chosen secrets never enter git. For CI-time needs, ephemeral values / dynamic provider auth avoid static credentials entirely. State access control is the backstop.
scenarios.hint: Where should the password live so neither git nor humans hold it?

scenarios.title: Blocking the open S3 bucket
scenarios.situation: A PR creates an S3 bucket with public-read ACL. You want CI to block policy violations automatically, not rely on reviewers spotting them.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces policy on Terraform plans?
choices: Policy as code: Sentinel (Terraform Cloud), OPA/Conftest (plan JSON), or Checkov/tfsec — evaluate the plan against rules in CI and fail the build
Reviewers must catch everything — automation can't
IAM policies prevent bad plans — nothing extra needed
Block all S3 buckets — simplest policy
scenarios.why: Policy-as-code evaluates 'terraform show -json tfplan' against rules (no public buckets, required tags, allowed regions, no 0.0.0.0/0 SGs) in CI — failing the pipeline before apply. It's the guardrail complement to human review: deterministic, always-on, and versioned with the code. Start with a small rule set and expand.
scenarios.hint: What can read a plan file and say 'no' before apply?

scenarios.title: Heard of Crossplane?
scenarios.situation: A teammate suggests Crossplane instead of Terraform: 'it lets us manage cloud resources with kubectl and GitOps natively.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest comparison?
choices: Crossplane brings IaC into the Kubernetes API (CRDs + controllers, GitOps-native reconciliation); Terraform has broader provider coverage and a mature state/plan workflow — choose by team model, not hype
Crossplane replaces Terraform entirely — migrate everything
They're identical — the name doesn't matter
Crossplane is only for databases — Terraform for the rest
scenarios.why: Crossplane = Kubernetes-native IaC: cloud resources as CRs, continuous reconciliation (self-healing like GitOps), composition into platform APIs (XRs). Strengths: k8s-native teams, control-plane model. Terraform strengths: provider breadth, plan/apply review workflow, huge ecosystem. Many orgs run both: Terraform for landing zones, Crossplane for app-team self-service.
scenarios.hint: What does 'reconciliation' give you that plan/apply doesn't?

lessons.title: IaC Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: Declarative IaC describes desired end state; the tool plans the actions and, crucially, compares current vs desired state on every run — creating only what's missing. Terraform excels at provisioning: declarative lifecycle of infrastructure resources with state.
Drift: mutable patching risks snowflake drift (failed patches, half-applied updates) and rollback means un-patching. Drift is any real-world change made outside Terraform.
Immutable infra means changes produce new images/instances rather than SSH-and-patch, which requires full codification (golden images or IaC) so any instance can be rebuilt identically.
Pets are unique, hand-maintained, and irreplaceable; cattle are identical and disposable.

Variables: together: variables in, locals compute, resources consume, outputs publish.
Validation: variable blocks support type constraints (string, number, list(string), object({...})) and validation { condition, error_message } blocks evaluated at plan.

lessons.title: State Management — Core concepts

Import: for bulk adoption, config-driven import blocks (import { to, id }) in Terraform 1.5+ make it reviewable in code.

simulations.brief: A teammate runs terraform plan on the shared staging workspace and the summary reads 'Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.' The database was supposed to be managed. Work the diagnostic steps to find why Terraform wants to destroy it.
simulations.debrief: A destroy plan almost always means config and state disagree about what should exist — removed blocks, wrong workspace, or wrong backend. Diagnose which one before touching anything, and make the correct context explicit in CI.

evidence:

  - aws_db_instance.main  (planned for destroy)

steps.explain: When a resource block disappears from configuration but the object still exists in state, plan proposes destroy. The fix is to restore the block (or move it intentionally with 'moved' blocks / state mv), not to delete state.
options: The database resource block was removed from the configuration, so Terraform plans to destroy the orphaned real object
The state file is corrupted and must be deleted
The AWS provider version changed and no longer supports RDS
Someone ran terraform taint on the database

evidence:

options: The teammate is on the wrong workspace — staging state lives in the 'staging' workspace, and 'default' has no DB in config scope
